intro: The reason to come is one tree, and two more on the same slope are worth the trip. The Hundred-Horse Chestnut, on Etna above Sant'Alfio, is put at roughly 2,200 years by a 2022 study, its trunk long since split into three stems that measure 10.5, 23 and 23.6 metres round and grow from one root system. Five hundred metres further up the same path stands the Ship's Chestnut, itself estimated at around 1,800 years, and the forest at Magazzeni holds a birch found only on Etna. Italy made the Hundred-Horse a national monument in 1965. Free, open all year.
meta_description: The Hundred-Horse Chestnut above Sant'Alfio is around 2,200 years old and grows from one root system as three vast stems. Free, open all year.
question_meta: Sant'Alfio's oldest tree is the Hundred-Horse Chestnut on Etna, dated to about 2,200 years in 2022. Where it stands and how to reach it.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Sant'Alfio is the Hundred-Horse Chestnut, the Castagno dei Cento Cavalli, a sweet chestnut on the eastern slope of Mount Etna at Via Castagno 100 Cavalli, about 30 kilometres north of Catania. A dendrological study by CREA in 2022 put it at roughly 2,200 years old, and both the Italian Wikipedia entry and the comune of Sant'Alfio's own page cite that figure. Older estimates drawn from folklore and earlier botanical work ran from 2,000 to 4,000 years. It is free to visit and open all year.
question_context: The 2,200 year figure comes from a dendrological study carried out by CREA, Italy's agricultural research council, in 2022. Both Wikipedia and the comune's own page repeat it, which is two citations of one study rather than two independent measurements, and worth knowing before treating the number as final. Older estimates, part folklore and part early botany, ranged from 2,000 to 4,000 years, and this page keeps that as the outer band rather than discarding it. Dating is complicated by what the tree has become. The original trunk split long ago into three stems growing from a single root system, measured at 10.5, 23 and 23.6 metres round, so there is no one trunk to work from and no intact core to read. A survey in 1780 ran a tape around the whole thing and came back with 57.9 metres, but that reading took in the branches. The register today records 22 metres of girth and 22 metres of height. Getting there means a car: it is about an hour from Taormina and half that from Catania, on mountain roads, and there is no useful bus.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Sant'Alfio?
faq.a: The Hundred-Horse Chestnut, the Castagno dei Cento Cavalli, dated to roughly 2,200 years by a CREA study in 2022. Older estimates run as high as 4,000 years.

faq.q: Is it one tree or three?
faq.a: One. The original trunk split long ago and the three huge stems that remain, 10.5, 23 and 23.6 metres round, all grow from the same root system. Standing in front of it, the instinct is to count three trees.
Yes, there is no entry charge and the site is open all year. There are some steps at the entrance, which may not suit wheelchair users.

By car. It is about 30 kilometres from Catania and 19 from Taormina, roughly 45 minutes to an hour on the SP59 and the mountain roads above Sant'Alfio. There is no practical public transport, so a car or a taxi is the realistic way to arrive.

trees.name: The Hundred-Horse Chestnut

location.neighbourhood: Sant'Alfio, eastern slope of Mount Etna

trees.story:
What looks like three enormous chestnuts on the slope above Sant'Alfio is one tree. The original trunk split long ago, and the three stems left standing, 10.5, 23 and 23.6 metres round, all grow from a single root system. A study by CREA, Italy's agricultural research council, put the whole thing at roughly 2,200 years old in 2022. Earlier estimates, part folklore and part botany, ran as high as 4,000.

The name comes from a story. A queen was caught in a storm on Etna with a hundred mounted knights, and the entire company is said to have sheltered under this one canopy. In 1780 someone arrived with a tape and reported 57.9 metres around, though that measurement took in the branches. The register today gives the trunk 22 metres and the tree 22 metres of height.

It has not had a quiet two millennia. Etna is directly above it, a fire took part of it in 1923, and it is still standing. Italy made it a national monument in 1965. In 1982 the State Forestry Corps worked through 22,000 trees and picked out 150 of exceptional value, this among them. UNESCO named it a Monument Messenger of Peace in 2006, and Italy voted it Tree of the Year in 2021.

Free, open all year, a few steps at the entrance.
trees.access: Free, no entry cost, open all year (comune.santalfio.ct.it, last updated 2026-03-26). Some steps at the entrance may not suit wheelchair users.
trees.transport: On Etna's eastern slope above Sant'Alfio, about 30km from Catania and 19km from Taormina. Roughly 45 minutes to an hour by car via the SP59/mountain roads; no practical public transport connection, so a car or taxi is the realistic way to reach it.

trees.name: The Ship's Chestnut

location.address: beside the path up from the Hundred-Horse Chestnut, about 500m further uphill, on the Sant'Alfio/Mascali boundary
location.neighbourhood: Carpineto, Mascali, eastern slope of Mount Etna

trees.story:
One source dates this chestnut to roughly 1,800 years old; a second confirms only that it is over a thousand, without putting a number on it. Either way it has been growing on Etna's slope above Sant'Alfio for a very long time, five hundred metres up the same path from the tree everyone comes for.

It carries two names, and neither is entirely flattering. Castagno della Nave, the Ship's Chestnut, describes the base, which flares out at the ground like a hull. Locals also call it arusbigghiasonnu, roughly wakes-you-from-sleep, for the racket the hundreds of birds roosting in its crown make at dusk.

The tree stands on private land, but right at the edge of the path, and the source describing it calls it clearly visible without stepping onto the property. No fee, no gate to pass, and no need to leave the route up to the Hundred-Horse Chestnut.

Reached the same way as its more famous neighbour: about an hour by car from Taormina, then on foot the last five hundred metres. Like most old chestnuts on this slope, it still drops chestnuts every October.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its base, which flares out like a ship's hull. It stands right at the edge of the path, about 500 metres uphill from the Hundred-Horse Chestnut, not set back in a garden.
trees.access: Stands on private land, but directly at the edge of the path up from the Hundred-Horse Chestnut, described by the source as clearly visible without entering the property. Free, no ticket.
trees.transport: Same trip as the Hundred-Horse Chestnut, about 500m further along the same path. Roughly an hour by car from Taormina; no practical public transport.

best_time.label: October, when the chestnuts come down

trees.name: The Etna Birch of Magazzeni

location.address: Magazzeni, Sant'Alfio, eastern slope of Mount Etna, approx. 1010m altitude

trees.story:
Nobody has dated this birch, and nobody should guess: its case for a place here rests on rarity rather than age. Betula aetnensis grows only on Mount Etna, a glacial relict left behind when the ice retreated, and it normally keeps to a band between 1,450 and 2,000 metres up the mountain. This one, registered in the forest at Magazzeni above Sant'Alfio, grows at just over 1,000.

Its bark runs unusually pale, almost white in patches, and that is not age showing, it is the ground: Etna's ash and lava carry too little lichen to darken a trunk the way rain and pollution would further down the slope.

Two separate registers, national and regional, agree on its size: 205 centimetres round and 12 metres tall.

It stands in open forest rather than behind any gate, a few kilometres from the two chestnuts that share this stretch of Etna's eastern slope, though no source describes a marked path leading to it specifically. Nobody has recorded when it was planted, or whether it planted itself. If you have stood in front of it and know either, tell us.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by bark that runs unusually pale, almost white in patches, among Etna's darker native trees, and by standing far lower on the mountain than most Etna birches, which keep to colder ground above 1,450 metres.
verified_sources: Regione Siciliana, Elenco degli alberi monumentali di Sicilia, updated 2024-11-07
trees.access: Free, in open forest on Etna's upper slopes within Sant'Alfio's territory. No gate or private boundary, though no source confirms a marked walking path to this specific tree.
trees.transport: A few kilometres from the two Sant'Alfio chestnuts, in the same Etna day-trip area; drivable together. No practical public transport, a car is needed.
